title: Can a New Credit Rating Agency Help Africans Borrow at Better Rates?
gist: The African Union launched the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) on Oct. 7 to counter what Africans call the 'Africa premium' from Moody's, S&P and Fitch, emphasizing local data, local-currency debt and rejection of the issuer-pays model. The authors see real differentiation but doubt its impact given home-bias concerns and global investors' need for cross-region comparability.

insights.claim: Moody's, S&P and Fitch together shape borrowing costs for more than 95 percent of the world's rated debt, spanning sovereigns, multilaterals and corporations.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: Any challenger faces an entrenched oligopoly with very high barriers to entry.
insights.quote: Together, these companies’ ratings shape borrowing costs for more than 95 percent of the world’s rated debt

insights.claim: 34 of Africa's 54 countries have a big-three credit rating, and 21 have issued Eurobonds since 1997 totaling more than $150 billion.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: Sizes the African sovereign Eurobond market that rating changes directly affect.
insights.quote: Now, 34 of the continent’s 54 countries have a credit rating from one of the big three agencies, and 21 countries have issued Eurobonds since 1997, amounting to more than $150 billion in financing.

insights.claim: Only Botswana, Mauritius and Morocco are rated investment grade by at least one of the big three agencies; all other rated African countries are junk grade.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: Almost all African sovereign debt sits in high-yield indices, shaping which investors can hold it.
insights.locator: But the vast majority of African

insights.claim: Fitch has no offices in Africa and S&P and Moody's historically had only one office each in South Africa, though S&P recently opened in Abuja and bought Agusto & Co., and Moody's acquired GCR Ratings in 2024.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: Incumbent rating agencies are buying local presence in response to competitive and political pressure.

insights.claim: A UNDP report estimates external credit ratings cost Africa $75 billion a year through inaccessible lending and disproportionate interest payments, and says Africa accounted for nearly half of all global sovereign downgrades in 2024.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: Quantifies the political grievance driving efforts to bypass the big three.
insights.quote: “In 2024, Africa accounted for nearly half of all global sovereign credit downgrades.”

insights.claim: During the height of COVID-19, 56 percent of rated African nations were downgraded versus a global average of 31.8 percent.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: African sovereign ratings are more procyclical in shocks, amplifying funding stress.

insights.claim: A 2023 IMF working paper found that, controlling for actual risk, financiers perceive sub-Saharan African countries as riskier than an objective assessment would suggest, confirming an 'Africa premium.'
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: If the premium is mispricing, African sovereign spreads may offer excess risk-adjusted return.

insights.claim: Afreximbank terminated its Fitch contract in January after repeated downgrades, and Dangote ended its Fitch contract after a 2024 downgrade.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: Major African issuers are dropping rating coverage, reducing transparency for bond investors.

insights.claim: The big three agencies deny mispricing African risk, saying they apply the same factors globally and that low ratings reflect poor economic, political and institutional health.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: The incumbent view is that spreads reflect fundamentals, not bias.

insights.claim: The African Union launched the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) on Oct. 7 to counter what it sees as overstated risk assessments that make African borrowing excessively expensive.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: A new continental rating benchmark could influence regional investor and DFI decisions.

insights.claim: AfCRA plans to emphasize local-currency debt ratings to unlock cross-African and regional funding from creditors unwilling to lend in dollars while sidestepping foreign-exchange risk.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: Could deepen African local-currency bond markets and reduce dollar dependence.

insights.claim: By rejecting the big three's issuer-pays model, under which non-paying entities go unrated, AfCRA aims to rate all sovereigns plus many private and multilateral actors.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: Broader coverage could expand the investable universe of rated African issuers.

insights.claim: AfCRA could counter home-bias accusations through high transparency, using published methodological formulas and local data rather than the big three's subjective judgments.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: Methodological transparency is the key test of whether investors will trust AfCRA ratings.

insights.claim: AfCRA's impact is likely limited because global lenders need apples-to-apples comparisons across regions and an Africa-only agency cannot provide them.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: Do not expect AfCRA ratings to compress Eurobond spreads in the near term.

insights.claim: Because AfCRA was built with the explicit goal of making Africa appear more investable, it has an inherent incentive to understate African borrowers' risk, on top of the general home-country bias of rating agencies.
insights.speaker: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
insights.so_what: Investors should discount AfCRA ratings for conflict of interest until a track record exists.
insights.quote: Inevitably, this creates an incentive for the AfCRA to artificially lower the risk profile of African borrowers.

source_meta.author: Dan M. Ford, Georgia Leanh Webb
